                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("38.180.107.76") or RemoteUrl has_any ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["38.180.107.76"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["env-check.daemontools.cc"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("38.180.107.76")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("38.180.107.76")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)

From poisoned search results to GPU mining: A cryptojacking campaign abusing ScreenConnect and Microsoft .NET utilities

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-05-26 21 use cases 11 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft exposes a cryptojacking campaign using SEO poisoning and ScreenConnect to target high-performance PCs, with malicious sites also surfaced through AI chatbots. [LLM] ZIP delivery from gleeze.com look-alike utility download sites (SEO/AI poisoning) Delivery High
Hunts browser-initiated ZIP downloads whose origin URL is a subdomain of the campaign's Dynu-hosted gleeze.com infrastructure (e.g. direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo). This is the initial-access foothold for the cryptojacking chain that impersonates CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, K-Lite and PDFgear. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named distribution infra (gleeze.com subdomains, directdownload.icu) corroborated by an ANY.RUN run of direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo and gbhackers/The Register reporting; 150+ subdomains all funnel the same ZIP, so the parent domain is a stable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://any.run/report/6468f63767212e0c1e4fe5d0eaa9137c4547ff173dc55b2d7fb1b2e445802d45/48172448-8ac9-4c17-8fef-bbf0c9a3d1e3 • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/10/cpuid_site_hijacked/

[LLM] DLL side-loading of autorun.dll by spoofed hardware-utility executables Installation High
Detects the legitimate (but trojanized-bundle) utility binaries — CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, PDFgear, K-Lite — loading a malicious autorun.dll from a user-writable folder via DLL search-order side-loading. Nine distinct autorun.dll variants were observed across the campaign; the module name + non-system host pairing is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious module name (autorun.dll) plus the article's enumerated host utilities; the image-load relationship from a user-writable path distinguishes side-loading from normal program startup. Datadog/Falcon use the autorun.dll file-write as a proxy since their FDR/Sysmon image-load fields aren't in scope here. Sentinel left blank: no standard Sentinel table carries Sysmon EID 7 image-load metadata in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] msiexec silently installing masqueraded vcredist_x64.dll (ScreenConnect packaged installer) Installation High
Detects autorun.dll's second stage: msiexec.exe silently installing a DLL named vcredist_x64.dll that poses as the Visual C++ Redistributable but is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. The DLL-as-MSI-payload plus silent flags is the article-specific behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim payload name vcredist_x64.dll passed to msiexec — a DLL is never a normal MSI target, making this near-zero-FP. Corroborated by gbhackers ('Microsoft Binary to Install RMM Tool') and cyberpress describing msiexec/MSI abuse to deploy the RMM. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] Unauthorized ScreenConnect client beaconing to directdownload.icu:8041 / 193.42.11.108 Command & Control High
Detects the abused ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe launched with the attacker's relay parameters (h=directdownload.icu, p=8041, session GUID b31c5795-9b66-4d20-ac8d-aad60d05852a, c=Crystaldeskinfo) or beaconing to C2 IP 193.42.11.108. This establishes the persistent remote access that could pivot to data theft or ransomware. Rationale: Uses the verbatim ScreenConnect service-invocation string from the article (relay host directdownload.icu, port 8041, exact session GUID, Crystaldeskinfo custom property) — these are unique to the attacker tenant, so any match is a confirmed compromise; the C2 IP 193.42.11.108 provides a network corroborator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/malware-crafted-through-connectwise-screenconnect-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] SimpleRunPE / RuntimeHost.exe dropped to hidden D3F4E2A1 install folder Installation High
Detects the process-hollowing dropper (SimpleRunPE.exe, SHA256 1b2555b0...) and its self-copy RuntimeHost.exe written into the campaign's hidden install folder keyed by identifier D3F4E2A1 (incl. fallback %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Caches\D3F4E2A1). Also pivots on the embedded PDB string and the C2 IP-resolved binary hash. Rationale: Combines the article's campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (used as folder name, mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc, and exclusion path), the dropper/persistence filenames, and the verbatim SHA256 — all unique strings that won't collide with legitimate software. PDB path (Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing-RUNPE) ties to the public PoC fork. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Watermwo/Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing • https://malware.news/t/from-poisoned-search-results-to-gpu-mining-a-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-and-microsoft-net-utilities/107339

| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Caches\", @"\AppData\", @"D3F4E2A1") or FileName in~ ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe")

[LLM] Defender exclusion added via Add-MpPreference for campaign install path Installation Medium
Detects the defense-evasion step where the malware runs PowerShell with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to call Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath, carving out its hidden D3F4E2A1 install location from Microsoft Defender scanning. Flags the exclusion-add behaviour, prioritising command lines that reference the campaign's Caches\D3F4E2A1 path. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim PowerShell evasion command (Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass) and boosts confidence when the exclusion path references the D3F4E2A1 / Caches install location. Kept as hunting because legit admins occasionally add exclusions. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = CommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: Run key WinSysCache Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's machine/user Run-key persistence value named WinSysCache under CurrentVersion\Run, which re-launches the hidden RuntimeHost.exe miner/loader at logon. The value name is a campaign-specific masquerade for 'Windows System Cache'. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Run-key value name WinSysCache under both HKLM and HKCU CurrentVersion\Run — a unique masquerade string that legitimate software does not use, making the registry-value name alone high-fidelity. [LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: 'Windows System Health' scheduled tasks Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's masqueraded scheduled tasks — 'Windows System Health' (logon), 'Windows System Health Monitor' (boot +1h), and 'Windows System Health Check' (every 5 min) — all running with highest privileges to relaunch the miner/loader. These exact task names are campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the three verbatim task names from the article's persistence table ('Windows System Health', '... Monitor', '... Check'); these names plus highest-privilege triggers are unique to the campaign and don't match any genuine Windows task. Defender query covers both schtasks.exe execution and the ScheduledTaskCreated telemetry for API-created tasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/

  | where AdditionalFields has "Windows System Health"

)

SecurityEvent

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] XWiki unauthenticated XAR import via REST POST /rest/wikis/{wikiName} (CVE-2026-33137)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] XWiki unauthenticated XAR import via REST POST /rest/wikis/{wikiName} (CVE-2026-33137) Exploitation High
Hunts successful, unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the XWiki REST XAR-import endpoint (/xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/]) that return 2xx, which is exactly the exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-33137 — the import runs with no auth/authz check, letting an attacker create or update wiki documents. The Authorization-header-absent + 2xx-status combination separates exploitation from legitimate authenticated XAR imports performed by admins/migration tooling. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's exact exploitation primitive — POST to /wikis/{wikiName} performing a XAR import with no auth check. Confirmed via XWiki docs/dev list that the real path is /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName} (POST, optional ?backup=&history= params, XAR in body), so the regex on /rest/wikis/<single-segment> plus 2xx plus absent Authorization header is high-fidelity for unauthenticated exploitation vs legitimate authenticated imports. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrvh-r3f2-9h4r • https://jira.xwiki.org/browse/XWIKI-23953 • https://www.xwiki.org/xwiki/bin/view/Documentation/UserGuide/Features/XWikiRESTfulAPI • https://devs.xwiki.narkive.com/KEuNSQkQ/xwiki-vote-add-rest-api-to-import-a-xar-file
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/rest/wikis/[^/?#]+/?($|\?)"   // /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/] XAR-import endpoint
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","202")            // import accepted/succeeded
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)              // CVE-2026-33137: import runs with NO auth header
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MuddyWater node.exe implant chain spawning PowerShell recon · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — MuddyWater Uses DLL Side-Loading in Espionage Campaign Targeting 9 Countries
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading rogue fmapp.dll · [LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: SentinelOne sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading rogue sentinelagentcore.dll · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MuddyWater C2 beacon to 157.20.182.49 and campaign domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SAM/SYSTEM hive theft via reg.exe save under MuddyWater node/PowerShell chain · [LLM] MuddyWater data exfiltration staging to sendit.sh file-transfer service · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading rogue fmapp.dll Installation High
Hunts the legitimately-signed Fortemedia audio binary fmapp.exe side-loading a malicious fmapp.dll (Operation Olalampo lineage) from a non-standard directory. The rogue DLL embeds ChromElevator and beacons to attacker IP 157.20.182.49, so a fmapp.exe running outside its Program Files install path is the high-fidelity tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact loader/DLL pair (fmapp.exe→fmapp.dll) plus the non-standard-path heuristic that separates the MuddyWater drop from legitimate Fortemedia audio software; pair documented by Group-IB (Operation Olalampo) and confirmed by Symantec. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/ • https://gbhackers.com/seedworm-apt-abuses-signed-binaries/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "fmapp.exe"
| where FileName =~ "fmapp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ModulePath = FolderPath, ModuleSHA256 = SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel has no native image-load table; pivot on process execution of the signed loader from a non-standard path
let legitPaths = dynamic(["C:\\Program Files","C:\\Program Files (x86)","C:\\Windows"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\fmapp.exe"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any (legitPaths))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: SentinelOne sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading rogue sentinelagentcore.dll Installation High
Hunts deliberate abuse of the signed SentinelOne binary sentinelmemoryscanner.exe to side-load a rogue sentinelagentcore.dll — chosen by MuddyWater specifically to evade signature-based detection. The rogue DLL name and any execution outside the SentinelOne install path is the discriminator. Rationale: sentinelmemoryscanner.exe → sentinelagentcore.dll is an exact named pair from the article; the rogue DLL name plus execution outside the SentinelOne directory makes this near-zero-FP, and Symantec/GBHackers confirm the deliberate security-product binary abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://gbhackers.com/seedworm-apt-abuses-signed-binaries/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ModulePath = FolderPath, ModuleSHA256 = SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel lacks an image-load table; detect the SentinelOne loader executing from a non-SentinelOne path
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\sentinelmemoryscanner.exe"
| where not(ActingProcessName has "SentinelOne" or ActingProcessName has "Sentinel Agent")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater node.exe implant chain spawning PowerShell recon Exploitation High
Hunts the MuddyWater node.exe-based implant chain that drops and launches PowerShell to perform reconnaissance, screenshot capture, SAM hive theft, privilege escalation and SOCKS5 reverse-proxy tunnelling. A node.exe parent spawning powershell.exe/cmd.exe is highly atypical of benign Node.js application behaviour. Rationale: Targets the article's specific node.exe→PowerShell implant chain (the unusual JS-runtime-as-loader pivot) rather than generic PowerShell; Symantec and BleepingComputer both describe node.exe dropping PowerShell recon scripts including SAM theft and SOCKS5 tunnelling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1113

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] SAM/SYSTEM hive theft via reg.exe save under MuddyWater node/PowerShell chain Actions on Objectives High
Hunts registry-hive export of the SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives via reg.exe save or PowerShell, used by the MuddyWater PowerShell scripts to harvest local credentials for lateral movement. Scoped to a node.exe/PowerShell parent lineage to keep it article-specific. Rationale: Implements the article's 'SAM hive theft' step with the canonical reg.exe save HKLM\SAM pattern (plus SYSTEM/SECURITY needed to decrypt it); machine-account exclusion and hive-name scoping keep FPs minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.004

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "reg.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "save"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security","\\sam ","\\security ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, GrandParent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"

| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater C2 beacon to 157.20.182.49 and campaign domains Command & Control High
Alerts on outbound connections to the MuddyWater C2 IP 157.20.182.49 (the address the side-loaded fmapp.dll connects to) and the campaign domains timetrakr.cloud and svc.wompworthy.com. Elevated confidence when the initiating process is one of the side-load loaders or node.exe. Rationale: 157.20.182.49 is the attacker IP the side-loaded fmapp.dll connects to (attributed by Huntress in the article); timetrakr.cloud and svc.wompworthy.com are pre-extracted campaign domains. IP/domain matches are inherently high-fidelity—validate the IP against threat-intel before broad alerting as only the article/Huntress cite it. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/muddywater-uses-dll-side-loading-in.html • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "157.20.182.49" or RemoteUrl has_any ("timetrakr.cloud","svc.wompworthy.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "157.20.182.49"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| union (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any ("timetrakr.cloud","svc.wompworthy.com") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater data exfiltration staging to sendit.sh file-transfer service Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts upload/staging of stolen data to the public file-transfer service sendit.sh, used by MuddyWater to exfiltrate collected data. Detects DNS/web connections to sendit.sh, especially from non-browser processes such as PowerShell, node.exe or curl. Rationale: sendit.sh is the specific public file-transfer service the article names as the data-staging destination; restricting to non-browser initiators (PowerShell/node/curl) separates exfil tooling from incidental user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/muddywater-uses-dll-side-loading-in.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")

         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'

            - '-NoProfile'

    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"

RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

let BadHashes = dynamic(["e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b", "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde", "128b58a2a2f1df66c474094aacb7e50189025fbf45d7cd8e0834e93a8fbed667", "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139", "74ab3838ebed7054b2254bf7d334c80c8b2cfec4a97d1706723f8ea55f11061f", "3ee7dab4ae4f6d4f16dfabb6f38faef370411a9fc00ff035844e54703b99600a", "bee79c3302b1a7afc0952842d14eff83a604ef00bfdae525176c16c80b2045f7", "d587959841a763669279ad831b8f0379f6a7b037dffc19deab5d41f37f8b5ffc", "b21c802775df0c0d82c8cfde299084abc624898b10258db641b820172a0ba29a", "589ecb0bb31adc6101b9e545a4e5e07ae2e97d464b0a62242a498e613a7740b6"]);

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MFA Prompt Bombing: Why Your Second Factor Isn't Saving You

The Hacker News
2026-05-26 10 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) was supposed to close a critical gap in identity security. It meant that, even if an attacker possessed the account credentials, they couldn't log in without the second factor. While that logic was sound, attackers have now figured out that they don't need to steal the second factor: they just need the user to hand it over. If your workforce authenticates with

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MFA push fatigue: repeated MFA prompt denials followed by an approval · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue MFA / security-info device registration after suspicious sign-in (Entra persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] MFA push fatigue: repeated MFA prompt denials followed by an approval Exploitation High
Hunts the MFA prompt-bombing pattern described in the article and the 2022 Cisco breach: an attacker with valid stolen credentials triggers a burst of push/MFA challenges that the user denies or that time out, then a single approval grants access. Detects clustered MFA-failure result codes for one user followed by a success in the same short window. Rationale: Uses the article's exact mechanism (repeated push-MFA prompts to wear the user down) expressed as the Entra failure codes 500121/50074/50076/50072 clustered then a success, the same pattern Cisco Talos documented in the 2022 breach. Threshold+temporal so alerting tier; no Sigma (correlation shape). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/recent-cyber-attack/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| extend Outcome = case(ErrorCode == 0, "success", ErrorCode in (500121, 50074, 50076, 50072), "mfa_prompt_failed", "other")
| where Outcome != "other"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize DeniedOrTimedOut = countif(Outcome == "mfa_prompt_failed"), Approved = countif(Outcome == "success"), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(Application, 10) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DeniedOrTimedOut >= 5 and Approved >= 1   // >=5 denied/timed-out MFA challenges then an approval in same 10m bucket
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend Outcome = case(ResultType == "0", "success", ResultType in ("500121","50074","50076","50072"), "mfa_prompt_failed", "other")
| where Outcome != "other"
| summarize DeniedOrTimedOut = countif(Outcome == "mfa_prompt_failed"), Approved = countif(Outcome == "success"), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DeniedOrTimedOut >= 5 and Approved >= 1   // 500121=MFA failed/denied, 50074/50076/50072=MFA required/prompted; >=5 then a success = fatigue
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:(500121 OR 50074 OR 50076 OR 50072)

[LLM] Rogue MFA / security-info device registration after suspicious sign-in (Entra persistence) Installation Medium
Hunts the persistence step from the article and Cisco breach: once a prompt-bombed login succeeds, the attacker enrolls their own device/authenticator for MFA so they retain access. Surfaces Entra ID 'registered security info' / device-registration audit events, ideally correlated to a recently risky or fatigue sign-in for the same user. Rationale: Targets the article's named persistence action — the Cisco attacker 'enrolled their own devices for MFA to maintain persistence' (confirmed by Talos) — via Entra audit OperationNames for security-info/device registration. Kept at hunting/high-FP because legitimate enrollment is common; intended to be triaged alongside the fatigue UC for the same user. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/recent-cyber-attack/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Microsoft Entra" or Application has "Azure Active Directory"
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Add registered devices","Register device","security info registration")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has_any ("registered security info","Add registered devices","Register device","security info registration")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIP, Target, Result, ResultReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MFA Security-Info / Device Registration in Entra ID (possible attacker persistence)
id: 7c3f1e2a-9b54-4d8e-bf1a-2e6c0d4a91f7
status: experimental
description: Detects registration of a new MFA method or device in Entra ID, the persistence step seen after MFA prompt-bombing in the 2022 Cisco breach. High base rate of legitimate enrollment; correlate with a preceding risky/fatigue sign-in.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
